ENT Clinical Note – Dr. Smith / Babylon Tele-consultation  

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 2-day history of lower abdominal pain; no identified food, medication, or environmental trigger.  
• Symptom timeline and progression: Pain began 2 days ago, persistent. Associated mild nausea, feels intermittently hot/sweaty. Reports mild pink discoloration of urine noted today. No vomiting. Constipation last week, now resolved.  
• ENT symptoms: Denies throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change/hoarseness, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, lip/tongue/uvular/facial swelling, ear pain/hearing changes, neck pain/swelling. No acid reflux symptoms.  
• Relevant past episodes and treatments: None. No prior similar abdominal or urinary episodes. No prior ED visits or adrenaline use.  
• Allergies: Amoxicillin (reaction details not documented).  
• Current medications: None. Contraceptive implant removed ≈1 year ago.  
• Social context: Lives with parents. Drinks alcohol ≈4×/week (≈1 beer each time). Non-smoker.

Objective:
• Observable swelling: None reported.  
• Airway/breathing: No respiratory distress or stridor reported.  
• Mental status: Alert, conversant.  
• Vitals/exam: Patient‐reported temp 37 °C one hour prior; no other vitals documented.  
• Presence of another person: Not stated.  

Assessment:
• No ENT pathology identified.  
• Clinical impression: Likely uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection causing lower abdominal pain and mild hematuria. ENT system review negative.

Plan:
• Prescription: 3-day course of oral antibiotics (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) sent to patient’s nominated pharmacy; begin immediately.  
• Safety-net advice: If pain worsens, fever develops, back pain appears, urinary symptoms progress, or new/worsening symptoms arise, contact service promptly for face-to-face review.  
• Follow-up: Re-consult if recurrence or no improvement after antibiotic course.  
• ENT-specific: None required; advised to report any new ENT symptoms such as throat swelling, voice changes, or breathing difficulty (red-flag escalation criteria discussed).

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing / expected elements: Detailed ENT examination findings (oropharynx, ears, neck), complete vital signs, antibiotic name/dose/route/frequency, detailed amoxicillin reaction history, documentation of urine dip or labs, availability of epinephrine auto-injector (not clinically indicated but standard ENT allergy check).  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minimal background noise; no significant inaudible sections.
